quotes.verbatim_quote:
All of the material that follows in this next section will be presented in C Major (no
accidentals). The assumption is that our readers will have (by now) developed the necessary
skills to make the needed adjustments to change the material to other 7-note scales. Here
are the choices available:

1. C Major Scale: No Accidentals
2. C Melodic Minor: Eb
3. C Harmonic Minor: Eb, Ab
quotes.why_load_bearing: This establishes the methodological rule that all exercises are in C Major but must be transposed by the student to melodic and harmonic minor variants.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
What follows may not be very interesting to a lot of readers. It consists of the
mathematical possibilities of voice-leading 3-part and 4-part chords within a 7-note scale
configuration. It’s really sort of a running journal of my R & D along these lines. Still, ’'ve
included it because a small percentage of our readers might find it interesting...
quotes.why_load_bearing: The author frames the generic voice-leading formulas as exhaustive mathematical derivations within a 7-note scale, establishing that the preceding exercises represent a curated subset of all possible voice-leadings.

quotes.topic: Generic VL key: A, B, C note labels
quotes.verbatim_quote:
Key:
A= Ist note
B = 2nd note
C = 3rd note
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the abstract notation system used for the generic voice-leading formulas, where chord tones are labeled A, B, C rather than scale degrees, enabling cycle-independent analysis.

quotes.topic: Only 3 generic VLs used in Vols I & II
quotes.verbatim_quote:
Note: Only 3 different
generic voice-leadings
were used out of 6!

Triads: cycle 6, cycle 7, cycle 5
3-part 4ths: cycle 6, cycle 7, cycle 5, cycle 4 (alt.)

Triads: cycle 2, cycle 4, cycle 3
3-part 4ths: cycle 2, cycle 4, cycle 3, cycle 5 (alt.)

3-part 4ths: cycle 2 (alt.), cycle 7 (alt.)
quotes.why_load_bearing: This reveals a key analytical finding — that the prior two volumes exhausted only 3 of 6 possible generic voice-leading patterns — contextualizing Volume III as expanding the remaining possibilities.

quotes.verbatim_quote: What follows are alternate voice-leadings for 4-part chords. All of these are different from any of the voice-leadings in either Volume I or Volume II. And just a reminder: all of the following examples could be tried in C melodic minor and C harmonic minor...
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage defines the scope and novelty of the alternate 4-part chord section, explicitly stating these voice-leadings are new to this volume and should be applied across scale types.

quotes.why_load_bearing: This illustrates the book's core analytical framework distinguishing intervallic motion (how far each voice moves) from functional role (which chord tone carries which voice), with the M.S.R.P. as the memorizable sequence.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
• Descends

• 3 other voices are incomplete 7th chord (no 3rd) but using c.t. voice-leading

quotes.why_load_bearing: This annotation teaches students to recognize when a voicing defies simple chord-tone analysis yet remains valid by ear, modeling the method's pragmatic approach to voice-leading theory.

quotes.topic: Duet texture with passing tones instruction
quotes.verbatim_quote: * 4-part; no passing tones Duet (top 2, bottom 2); add p.t.. ¢ NICE in Harmonic minor!
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives a specific performance instruction — splitting 4-part voicings into two-voice duets and adding passing tones — plus a stylistic recommendation for harmonic minor application.
